ACT-EN2C-P1-Q01.note: Conventions. I pick the comma: 'a wooden double of the part' renames 'a pattern' and a nonrestrictive appositive takes a comma. But 'pattern:' is defensible under edited American English and the item should drop. The colon rule is that the material BEFORE the colon must be a complete sentence - not that the clause immediately preceding it must be independent. What precedes here is 'The second bay past the scale house belongs to Odile Bracht, whose bench turns out no parts, only a pattern,' which is a complete sentence (main clause plus a relative clause). Chicago 6.61-6.63 expressly licenses a colon introducing an amplification or appositive after such a sentence, and the trailing participial phrase survives it: '...only a pattern: a wooden double of the part, pressed into damp sand to leave a hollow behind it.' It arguably reads BETTER than the key, because the key produces four commas in one sentence, two of them ('parts, only a pattern, a wooden double') stacked in a way that briefly reads as a list. The explanation's stated grounds are themselves wrong - it rejects the colon because "'whose bench turns out no parts' is a relative clause that cannot stand alone," which applies the test to the wrong span. Fix by making the pre-colon span genuinely non-independent, or by replacing the colon distractor with a dash-vs-comma contrast. Four-words-after shortcut: PARTIAL - 'a wooden double of' announces a following noun phrase within two words, but a noun phrase is compatible with comma, colon and dash alike, so the local window narrows the field without deciding it.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q02.note: Conventions, subject-verb agreement across an intervening prepositional phrase. 'Half the patterns' takes its number from the object of the partitive ('patterns'), so the verb is plural; 'on her rack' cannot supply the subject. No convention rescues a second option: 'is' and 'has been' are singular, and 'was' is both singular and past, which would also break the essay's present tense ('belongs', 'turns out'). The partitive-with-plural rule is uncontested in every American usage authority. Four-words-after shortcut: CLEAN, and this is the best-built Conventions item in the batch for that reason. The window after the blank is 'older than the furnace' - a comparative that is number-neutral and tense-neutral. The evidence sits four to six words BEFORE the blank and must be read across the distractor phrase 'on her rack', which is exactly the work the subskill names.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q03.note: Knowledge of Language. 'gradually' is right and nothing else is arguable: 'suddenly' and 'quickly' are contradicted outright, and 'intermittently' is killed by 'the whole time' in the same sentence. Exclusive - but the distractors are weak because all three fail on the same single cue rather than on three different ones, so the item collapses to one test rather than four. Four-words-after shortcut: FULL HIT, and the clearest instance in the batch. The four words after the blank are 'over the eleven hours' - a stated duration of eleven hours defeats 'suddenly', 'quickly' and 'intermittently' simultaneously, and a solver who reads no further than word four is done. That is why I grade this easy against a real 42-second-per-item section despite the author's 'medium'. To repair it without touching the key, move the duration out of the blank's sentence (put 'eleven hours' in the preceding or following sentence) so the precision judgement has to be carried across a sentence boundary.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q04.pick: Yes, because it opens the distinction that paragraph 3 builds its whole account on.
ACT-EN2C-P1-Q04.note: Production of Writing, adding material. The key is right on the merits: paragraph 2 ends with a single oversize allowance, paragraph 3 immediately splits that allowance by metal and issues Bracht a separate rule for each, so the added sentence is the hinge. Exclusive holds, but only just, and for a reason the author should hear: the strongest objection to the addition is not on the ballot. The added sentence opens with the definite 'The fraction' while paragraph 2 has named no fraction at all (it says 'a hair too small' and 'oversize'); the first fraction in the essay, an eighth of an inch per foot, does not appear until paragraph 3. A careful reader can therefore mount a real 'No' - the sentence refers back to something that has not been introduced - and would then find that neither No option says that. C asserts paragraph 2 'has settled on one fixed fraction' (it has not) and D asserts the metals are 'not a subject this essay returns to' (they return in paragraphs 4 and 5). Both are false on the text, so I vote exclusive true; but the item is one edit from being unanswerable, and the cheap fix is to have paragraph 2 mention the allowance as a fraction so 'The fraction' has an antecedent. ON THE AUTHOR'S BLIND-LEAK FLAG: I agree, and the leak is worse than the 50% they estimate. The stem quotes the candidate sentence in full, so a blind solver reads 'The fraction is not the same for every metal' and sees it contains no fraction - option A ('gives the reader the exact fraction') is refuted by the stem alone, with no passage. That is not a distractor, it is a free elimination, and it leaves a 1-of-3 field before any direction prior is applied. Add the standing ACT prior that a quoted sentence offered for addition is usually worth adding, plus B being the only option that assigns the sentence a structural function, and I would expect a blind solver well above the 76% stratum mean rather than at the 50% floor the four-option frame was built to hold. The frame (two Yes, two No, one paragraph cited each, matched length) controls direction and does nothing about content, because the stem hands over the sentence itself. The repair is at the option level: make A describe something the quoted sentence could plausibly do, so that eliminating it requires the passage.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q05.note: Conventions, sentence boundaries. 'Bronze shrinks' and 'aluminum shrinks nearly twice as much as gray iron does' are both independent, so the comma is a splice and the bare form a run-on; the semicolon is the only mark here that joins them. The colon is the one option with a structural licence - what precedes it IS an independent clause - and it fails on sense rather than on structure: the second clause sets a different metal beside the first rather than explaining or itemizing it. That is a meaning judgement the real ACT tests routinely, so I hold exclusive true. Separate note for the author, not a grading vote: 'Bronze shrinks' is semantically bare as a clause - shrinks how much? - and the sentence reads as though it lost a word ('Bronze shrinks more,'). Fixing the punctuation leaves that oddity in the passage. Four-words-after shortcut: FULL HIT. The second word after the blank is 'shrinks', so 'aluminum shrinks' delivers a complete subject-plus-verb inside the window and forces a boundary mark; only the colon-versus-semicolon choice needs anything further, and even that is settled by word four ('nearly twice'), which signals comparison rather than explanation. A solver never needs paragraph 3.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q06.note: Conventions, parallel structure. 'would mean' governs three gerund phrases; the first two are 'doing the arithmetic on every dimension' and 'checking it against the drawing', so the third must be 'weighing'. No convention licenses a second answer: the infinitive breaks a series whose form is already fixed twice over, and 'weighed'/'weighs' are finite verbs with no subject available. I grade this medium rather than the author's hard - a three-item -ing series with the odd one out in final position is among the most recognizable shapes on the section, and the two finite-verb distractors are eliminable on sight without doing the parallelism work at all. Four-words-after shortcut: CLEAN, and the second well-built Conventions item here. The window after the blank is 'a scrapped pour against', which carries no form information; the governing evidence is the two gerunds roughly twelve and twenty words upstream, so the item genuinely requires backward reading across the full series.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q07.note: Production of Writing, transitions. The prior sentence says what Kessel has never done (put the scheme in a manual) and this sentence says what occupies that place (a strip of tape), so the connector must mark substitution. 'Therefore' would make the absent manual the cause of the tape; 'In addition' would add the tape to a manual the prior sentence denies exists. I flag 'Still' as the one option worth arguing about, and record why I still vote exclusive: a concessive reading is constructible - 'Kessel has never written this down. Still, [there is a record:] the only list is a strip of tape' - since the sentence does assert that some list exists. What defeats it is 'the only', which frames the tape as a deficiency continuous with the missing manual rather than in contrast to it; a concession needs the second clause to push back, and this one piles on. That is a 'most logical' comparison, which the stem asks for, not a convention dispute, so exclusivity survives. Medium rather than the author's easy: eliminating 'Still' takes the reasoning above, not a reflex. Not a Conventions or KoL item, so the four-word rule does not apply; for completeness, the window after the blank ('the only list of what') does contain 'the only', which is the deciding word - transitions items are not covered by the recorded defect, but the author may want to know the discriminator sits inside the same four-word window anyway.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q08.note: Conventions, possessives. The door belongs to the single shop the essay describes throughout, so the singular possessive is required; the bare plural marks no possession, 'shops'' invents multiple shops, and 'shop' leaves an attributive noun with no ownership marking. Nothing defensible in second place. Four-words-after shortcut: PARTIAL. 'door' sits one word after the blank and settles that SOME possessive is needed, which eliminates two of four options inside the window; what the window cannot settle is singular versus plural, and that requires the essay's one-shop frame. One leak the author may not have noticed and it is not in the four-word window: paragraph 5 already prints 'the shop's own allowance' in the same passage, so a solver can pattern-match the exact target form off another sentence without reasoning about number at all. Consider changing that paragraph-5 phrase to avoid handing over the answer.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q09.note: Knowledge of Language, word precision, and the best-built item in the batch on distractor quality: the four options are genuine near-neighbours that separate on whether the figure has a basis and whether it is meant to be tested. What the paragraph describes is a published figure for the nearest metal, cut to, then corrected against a casting measured cold - a value taken from a source and deliberately checked, which is an estimate. 'guess' and 'hunch' both deny it any basis, and 'assumption' names something taken for granted, which is the opposite of a figure the shop sets out to test. I considered No Change seriously, since the figure is borrowed from a DIFFERENT metal and 'guess' is colloquially fair for that; what settles it is that the stem asks for the most precise word and the paragraph supplies both the source and the verification, so the more specific term wins. Exclusive, but the margin is the narrowest of the ten. Four-words-after shortcut: FULL HIT, by one word. The blank ends its sentence and the next begins 'Bracht takes the published' - 'published' is the fourth word after the blank and is precisely the resolving evidence, since a published figure is exactly what separates 'estimate' from 'guess' and 'hunch'. The shortcut is slightly harder to exploit than in Q03 or Q05 because it requires reading 'published figure' as a basis rather than spotting a form cue, but it is inside the window and the author should treat it as a hit. Moving 'published' later in its clause would cost nothing and close it.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q10.note: Production of Writing, sentence placement. The added sentence states the standing condition that the whole paragraph answers, so it belongs ahead of the paragraph's opening, where the new alloy and its first sized-from-a-guess pattern immediately follow from it. [B] would explain a problem the paragraph has already started solving, and [C] would cut the wait-then-measure procedure in half. [D] is the option that nearly takes the item and the author should know how close it comes: placed there, the sentence sets up a general claim and the silicon-bronze sentence supplies its instance, with a direct lexical hook ('arrives with a published figure' / 'nobody upstate had a figure for'), and general-then-example is a recognized arrangement. I vote exclusive anyway, on the ground that the premise has to precede the procedure it motivates - by [D] the paragraph has already run the entire guess-cut-wait-measure sequence that presupposes the missing figure, so the sentence arrives as a late restatement of what the reader has just watched happen, and the silicon-bronze closer already carries the point in concrete form, making the addition redundant rather than introductory. That reasoning is real but it is a two-step, which is why I grade this hard and rate the distractors strong. Note for the author: this item and Q09 operate on the same sentence at [A], which is fine as written - Q10 is solvable whichever way Q09 is answered - but watch that no later edit makes one depend on the other. The four-word rule does not apply to a placement item.
